---
title: Write a plugin with the AI
description: Ask the assistant in the app to write a PLUGIN.md plugin with you. It reads the language reference, validates the draft, tries read-only tools against the live service, and opens the usual review sheet, where you decide whether to install.
icon: Sparkles
---

A plugin document is plain text, so the AI assistant in the app can write one with you. For
example, you can ask for "a plugin for the gym booking site". The result is a `PLUGIN.md` folder
that you review and then install, or discard.

You need only the app and a configured AI model. No computer is required, although you will want
one later if you publish the plugin.

The assistant does this work through the tools of a built-in plugin called **Plugins** (id
`plugins`). None of these tools can install anything without your confirmation.

## The tools

The assistant uses five tools. The first four only read, and the last one opens a sheet for you.

**`plugins.reference`** (read) returns the whole plugin language on one page: the manifest, steps,
expressions, the standard library, host abilities, limits and an example. The assistant reads it
when it is about to write or edit a plugin. It is not part of every prompt, so it takes up no space in
other conversations.

**`plugins.validate`** (read) checks a draft folder with the same loader the app uses. The draft is
passed as `{ files: { "PLUGIN.md": "…", "tools/x.yaml": "…" } }`. The tool returns
`{ ok: true, id, version, tools, widgets, campus, network, abilities }` when the draft is valid. Otherwise
it returns `{ ok: false, issues }`, and each issue names the file and step where the problem is.

**`plugins.tryTool`** (read) runs one **read** tool of a draft for real, without installing the
draft. It sends live requests, uses your campus sessions for the services the draft declares, and
gives the tool a throwaway store. Tools with the `write`, `money` or `public` effect can't be tried
this way. The results are treated as untrusted data.

**`plugins.source`** (read) returns the files of an installed plugin document, so the assistant can
explain, fix or copy it. Built-in TypeScript plugins have no document, so this tool doesn't work for
them.

**`plugins.install`** (write) opens the app's review sheet for a link (a GitHub folder or a
`PLUGIN.md` URL) or for a draft (`{ files }`). It only opens the sheet. You make the decision there.

The Plugins plugin asks before it runs `write` tools by default. Unless you have changed that mode,
the assistant therefore also checks with you before it opens the sheet.

## How a plugin is written [#the-flow]

<Steps>
<Step>

### Describe what you want

Say what the plugin should do. If you know which page or API it should use, say that too. If it is a
campus service, mention it: the plugin will call the service with your signed-in session and will
never see your password.

</Step>
<Step>

### The assistant drafts and validates [#the-agent-drafts-and-validates]

The assistant reads `plugins.reference`, then writes `PLUGIN.md` and the tool files. It calls
`plugins.validate` after each change and keeps fixing the draft until no issues are left.

</Step>
<Step>

### It tries the read tools

`plugins.tryTool` runs a read tool against the real service. You see actual results before anything
is installed, which tells you whether the plugin really works.

</Step>
<Step>

### You review and install

`plugins.install` opens the same review sheet you see for an install link. It shows whether the
plugin is official or community; the campus services, websites and app features it can reach; and
every tool with its effect. A draft written in chat counts as a community plugin. Nothing is
installed until you tap *Install*.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Changing an installed plugin

To change an installed plugin document, ask the assistant to fix or extend it. It reads the files
with `plugins.source`, edits them, validates the result, and opens the review sheet again with the
new version.

If you paste a plugin link in the chat, the assistant opens the review sheet for it with
`plugins.install { link }`.

## Share what you made

The assistant's draft is an ordinary plugin folder. To share it, or to let it update from a link,
put the folder in a public GitHub repository. The folder's URL becomes its install link (see
[Your first plugin](/en/docs/build/quickstart#share-it)). Before you publish, run the
[author CLI](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins#test) on a computer and add recorded tests.

## Safety

- The assistant never installs anything by itself. `plugins.install` only opens the review sheet.
- `plugins.tryTool` runs only read tools, reaches only what the draft declares, and keeps nothing.
- An installed draft follows the same rules as any community plugin. Its `write`, `money` and
  `public` tools ask first, and its results reach the AI as data, never as instructions.

The language itself is covered in [Declarative plugins](/en/docs/build/declarative-plugins).
[Permissions](/en/docs/concepts/permissions) explains how the permission modes work.
